articles.title: The 3pm football blackout: outdated or still relevant in 2026?
articles.summary: After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
articles.body:
After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?

With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.

There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first .

But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.

Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.

With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.

Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.

BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.

How Match of the Day ushered in the blackout

It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day .

Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.

Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?

Burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.

A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.

Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.

Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.

Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.

Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.

This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".

Why does no other country have the blackout?

Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.

No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.

It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.

Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

This misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.

Could you imagine English football replicating this?

In Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.

In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.

In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.

So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.

The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.

The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.

There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.

Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said there were no plans to remove the blackout.

But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.

Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon .

It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.

So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record £6.7bn - an increase of 4%.

However, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.

Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.

Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?

If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.

Could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.

Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.

'Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League'

There is a danger that the issue of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, says there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".

"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex said.

"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game."

BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.

It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.

Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, who attend non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.

The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.

Nicky Bloom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the issue is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.

"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Bloom told BBC Sport.

"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.

"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.

"The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters."

Bloom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".

Streaming could still be an opportunity for some clubs

Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.

Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.

North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.

Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.

"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton said.

"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours."

Ashington, which have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already see the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.

For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.

There is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.

Added to that, there are now many weekends when when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.

For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.

Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.

But this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.

Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.

articles.title: Elikia Mbinga: From Ajax's academy to millions of Spotify streams
articles.summary: Former Ajax academy player Elikia Mbinga tells BBC Sport how he swapped football for music after playing with some Premier League stars.
articles.body:
Elikia Mbinga dreamed of becoming a professional footballer and playing in sold-out arenas after captaining an Ajax side brimming with future stars.

But at 25, his life has taken an unexpected turn. Rather than showcasing his creativity on the pitch, Mbinga is making a name for himself through music.

He has become one of the most successful emerging afrobeat artists in the Netherlands, with more than 30 million Spotify streams.

It is a world away from Ajax's famed De Toekomst academy, where he trained alongside a host of Dutch talents who have since made their mark in the Premier League - from the Timber brothers to Ryan Gravenberch and Brian Brobbey.

It is clear the lessons Mbinga learned during his esteemed footballing education have helped shape his identity as an artist.

"As a footballer, I played in midfield and was a very creative player. That was my style on the pitch, and I try to bring that same creativity to my music," he tells BBC Sport.

"I want to experiment with songs, be as creative as possible and develop a sound of my own."

'You don't know they're going to become stars'

By the age of 17, Mbinga was living the dream of many aspiring footballers in the Netherlands.

After impressing at boyhood club PEC Zwolle, he earned a move to Ajax and began a new life in Amsterdam away from his mother and seven siblings.

During his four seasons at the club, he shared the dressing room with brothers Quinten and Jurrien Timber, now of Crystal Palace and Arsenal, who joined Ajax from Feyenoord around the same time Mbinga arrived from Zwolle.

"We had a feeling that we had joined this journey together," Mbinga recalls. "We stepped in together. Already then, you could see that Quinten and Jurrien were like machines. They were built like machines from a young age."

He remembers the technical elegance of Liverpool midfielder Gravenberch and the physical prowess of striker Brobbey, who went on to score 56 goals in 163 appearances for Ajax's first team before moving to Sunderland last September.

Mbinga also had the opportunity to test himself against some of Europe's biggest clubs, including Real Madrid, Manchester United and Manchester City.

At one point, he even captained the group and saw little to separate them in terms of ability. However, their careers would take very different paths.

"In terms of talent, there wasn't really a big difference at the time," he says.

"Then, maybe two or three years later, Ryan Gravenberch had already made his first-team debut for Ajax. So it's all about development, right? And the same goes for the other guys."

Looking back, Mbinga now deeply treasures those years and the opportunity to have played alongside such talented footballers.

"I played with some amazing, talented players, and at the time, you already knew that they were really talented, right? It's the highest level," he says.

"But you don't know that they're going to become Premier League stars in the upcoming years. So that's amazing to look back at."

After struggling to break through, Mbinga returned to PEC Zwolle in 2021 at the age of 20, where the familiar, less pressurised surroundings prompted him to consider life beyond football and his ambition to build something of his own.

"I think it was also part of the personal growth. I really liked the music. I also liked looking up to the other artists at the time who were popping," Mbinga says.

"For me, it was also a dream to do something in music, create my own songs. But at that time, I was really talented with football, but I couldn't make music yet."

Mbinga made his professional debut for his local side in September 2021, coming off the bench against Ajax, of all teams, in the Eredivisie.

But the youngster would make just five further first-team appearances as Zwolle were relegated, before dropping down the Dutch football pyramid.

He ended up playing semi-professionally in the fourth tier to fund his music career.

"When I made my professional debut, everything went really well. I signed the contract and everything," he says.

"But the purpose of creating something for myself in terms of music, being very creative, was getting stronger."

Five years on, that gamble is paying off. He has almost 500,000 monthly Spotify listeners, while his 2024 track Mentality has surpassed 16 million streams.

Every now and again, making music offers Mbinga a thrill similar to that he once chased on the football pitch.

"For me, all the achievements in music are like I'm scoring a goal or I'm giving an assist or playing a good match," he laughs.

"And of course, if one of my songs really takes off, then it feels like I'm scoring the winning goal in a very important game - like a final!"

Touring the world and reconnecting with former team-mates

Although Mbinga remains content with his decision not to pursue a career in professional football, he remains closely connected to the sport that shaped his life.

Earlier this month, he travelled to the United Kingdom to promote his new album, First of a Kind, allowing him to reunite with former Ajax team-mates Jurrien and Quinten Timber.

Mbinga attended an Arsenal Champions League match at Emirates Stadium and a Premier League Crystal Palace game at Selhurst Park.

"I'm really focused on creating this world for the people, for the fans," says Mbinga. "Creating a world that can unite football and music - like a creative bridge."

Another footballer supporting his musical journey is Spain forward Ansu Fati, who plays for AS Monaco.

The pair met as teenagers at a youth tournament in Europe when Fati was at Barcelona and have remained close friends ever since.

In February, Mbinga released a song dedicated to the forward and the challenges he has faced since breaking through at Barcelona in 2019.

Fati was seen as one of the new generation of La Masia stars at Camp Nou, making 51 appearances for the first team in 2022-23.

But he was loaned to Brighton the following season and struggled for minutes on his return to the Catalan giants, eventually joining Monaco on loan last season in a deal that became permanent in the summer.

Mbinga wrote the track in 2024 but agreed with Fati to release it only when the "time was right".

"You know what's crazy? Seeing him again and seeing everything that he's gone through," he recalls. "We went out to eat, went out for dinner, and then he was playing my song in the car, singing it lyric for lyric.

"I was like, 'wow, this life is crazy, man'."

articles.title: La felicidad plena de Nico Paz goleando con Argentina: ¿Por qué decidió no jugar con España?
articles.standfirst: "Estoy muy feliz, representar esta camiseta (Argentina) es lo máximo. Estoy muy feliz"
articles.summary: "Estoy muy feliz, representar esta camiseta (Argentina) es lo máximo. Estoy muy feliz"
articles.body: El canario Nico Paz, jugador del Como 1907 al que el Real Madrid podría recuperar con una cláusula unilateral de 80 millones de euros, marcó dos goles en 45 minutos en el triunfo de Argentina contra Costa Rica por 7-0 en el Mario Alberto Kempes de Córdoba (Argentina). "Estoy muy feliz, representar esta camiseta es lo máximo. Sobre todo en días como hoy, con toda la gente y todo el cariño que se ha sentido hoy. Muy feliz", declaró tras el partido. El emergente centrocampista, que ya suma seis goles con Argentina, confesó que "poco a poco me estoy encontrando mejor, estoy divirtiéndome más en el campo", y destacó que "creo que tenemos un equipo con una calidad increíble y para mí en el campo es más fácil hacer el juego que hago en mi club". Nico Paz es el principal candidato a heredar la mítica camiseta con el número 10 de la albiceleste que con anterioridad lucieron genios con Leo Messi, Diego Armando Maradona, Mario Kempes o Juan Román Riquelme. "La verdad que no pienso en ello (en heredar la camiseta con el 10), lo que pienso es en disfrutar días como hoy... Divertirme en el campo que lo que más amo es jugar al fútbol y encima representando a la selección y representando a tanta gente... juego para eso y quiero seguir haciéndolo", respondió el ex del Madrid, que jugó con el número 18 y lleva cuatro goles en solo 48 días al marcar ante Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Benín y Costa Rica. Nico Paz, que es hijo del exfutbolista argentino Pablo Paz, nació en Santa Cruz de Tenerife el 8 de septiembre de 2004. En 2023 Pablo Paz, que en el fútbol español militó en Tenerife y Valladolid, explicó en Radio MARCA Tenerife por qué su hijo Nico Paz juega con Argentina y no con España. "¿Argentina o España? Nico no tuvo que decidir, la Selección española nunca lo ha llamado. Surgió la oportunidad y a Nico le gustaba mucho, así que la aprovechó. Pudo entrenar con Messi, su ídolo", declaró Pablo Paz tras una convocatoria de Nico con la sub 20 de Argentina. En ese momento Pablo Paz comentó qué haría Nico Paz en el caso de que la absoluta de España lo llamase: "Si España lo llamara, no sé qué haría Nico. Ahora mismo, si me preguntas a mí, creo que se quedaría con Argentina, pero depende de los momentos, situaciones, lo que le digan. Él elegirá lo que sienta". Nico, uno de los llamados 'Europibes' de Scaloni, eligio´a la selección de Argentina. "Yo nací en España. Amo a los dos países, pero al final decidí representar a Argentina. Creo que es el país que más me representa, por cómo se vive el fútbol y por mi padre, que es un orgullo seguir sus pasos", reconoció el propio Nico Paz en 'D Selección' de 'DSports Radio'.

articles.title: El caso de Pedro Cortés desde dentro: "Te voy a comer enterito"
articles.standfirst: MARCA habla con la cantera del Valencia y con el abogado del menor para que nos explique como trabajaron en este caso donde el expresidente fue condenado por abusar sexualmente de un canterano
articles.summary: MARCA habla con la cantera del Valencia y con el abogado del menor para que nos explique como trabajaron en este caso donde el expresidente fue condenado por abusar sexualmente de un canterano
articles.body: No siempre el agresor está dentro del vestuario. A veces llega en un coche, con un apellido conocido y décadas de prestigio detrás. En noviembre de 2020, un futbolista de 16 años de la cantera del Valencia subió al vehículo de Pedro Cortés, presidente del club entre 1997 y 2001 y, en ese momento, delegado de la selección española. Lo que pasó durante ese trayecto acabó en una condena por abuso sexual a un menor. Si el caso de Amigos 80 muestra lo que ocurre cuando el agresor es dueño del club, este muestra otra cara del mismo problema, la del hombre poderoso que se mueve alrededor del fútbol base sin formar parte de su estructura. Como complemento a este especial, MARCA ha hablado con el abogado de la familia del jugador, que nunca ha querido dar su nombre, y con Borja Eroles, coordinador de Operaciones de la Academia VCF y responsable de su protocolo de protección a la infancia. La confianza venía de antes. El jugador había firmado un contrato de representación con una agencia dirigida por un familiar de Cortés. Eso le dio al expresidente un contacto habitual con el chico y, según la Fiscalía, una "relación de confianza". El patrón se parece al que describía la psicóloga Raquel Molero en el reportaje principal: "El abuso casi nunca empieza con algo claramente sexual, sino con alguien cercano que presta una atención especial". En noviembre de 2020, Cortés invitó al jugador a comer con su familia en un restaurante de Valencia. Según el relato de la acusación, durante la comida le susurró al oído: "Te voy a comer enterito". Después se ofreció a llevarlo en su coche a la Ciudad Deportiva de Paterna, donde el chico vivía en la residencia del club. En el trayecto, siempre según la acusación, Cortés le puso la mano en el muslo, fue subiéndola hacia la zona genital y llegó a tocarle el pene. El chico le apartó la mano. La respuesta del expresidente, de más de 70 años, fue que la vida solo se vive una vez y hay que disfrutarla. Después llegaron los mensajes de WhatsApp. La familia denunció en noviembre de 2020. La investigación se conoció el 21 de enero de 2021, y ese mismo día Cortés negó los hechos a través de un comunicado de su abogado y dimitió como delegado de la selección en la Federación Española. En octubre de 2021, el Juzgado de Primera Instancia e Instrucción número 1 de Paterna lo procesó por un presunto delito de abuso sexual a un menor de 16 años. El juicio se celebró a puerta cerrada el 23 de febrero de 2023 en el Juzgado de lo Penal número 3 de Valencia. Cortés negó los tocamientos, pero admitió ser el autor de los mensajes. La Fiscalía pedía dos años de prisión y la acusación particular, dos años y medio. La sentencia se hizo pública el 3 de marzo de 2023. El juez lo condenó a un año y diez meses de prisión por abuso sexual. También le impuso una indemnización de 6.000 euros para la víctima, la prohibición de acercarse a menos de 200 metros del joven o comunicarse con él durante tres años y dos años de libertad vigilada. El joven nunca ha dado la cara en público. Su abogado, Mariano Oliver, lo explica con sencillez: "Cuando una persona lo que quiere es justicia y no busca ni relevancia ni notoriedad pública, evidentemente trata de permanecer en el anonimato". Todo empezó con una conversación. Tras lo ocurrido en el coche, el chico llegó a la residencia del Valencia y habló, como hacía casi a diario, con una amiga de toda la vida. Ella le dijo que debía contárselo a sus padres. "Con un criterio excelente", subraya el letrado. El joven lo hizo y, a la vez, lo puso en conocimiento de su tutor en la residencia, una figura que tienen todos los canteranos que viven en la Ciudad Deportiva. La familia llegó al despacho por referencias, con la denuncia ya presentada. "Lo primero que pensamos fue en la situación tan compleja en la que estarían el joven y su familia, porque no es fácil dar este paso, sobre todo frente a personas tan notorias y con tanta influencia", recuerda. Son dudas que se repiten en casi todas las víctimas: "¿Me creerán?, ¿cómo voy a poder probarlo?, ¿cómo me va a afectar esto en el futuro?, ¿tendré que soportar un señalamiento público?". El abogado no esconde que fue "un proceso muy difícil". Enfrente estaba "una persona con una notoriedad y una influencia muy grandes en el mundo del fútbol", expresidente de uno de los grandes clubes de España y con fuertes vínculos federativos. Según su relato, hubo intentos de desacreditar al joven "en lo personal, incluso en su comportamiento deportivo". La defensa presentó múltiples recursos y llegó a sostener que los mensajes de WhatsApp estaban sacados de contexto o incompletos. La respuesta de la acusación fue aportar los chats íntegros y pedir su cotejo ante el letrado de la Administración de Justicia. "La defensa no pudo aportar ningún listado de mensajes que fuera distinto del aportado por nosotros", afirma. Los describe como "absolutamente inapropiados, de un innegable contenido sexual", impropios de la relación entre un hombre de más de 70 años y un menor. Cada recurso ganado, cuenta, les confirmaba que había que "llevarlo hasta el final". Sobre la condena, el letrado recuerda que los hechos se juzgaron como abuso sexual, con una pena prevista de entre uno y tres años, porque la reforma de la ley del "solo sí es sí" llegó con el procedimiento ya en marcha. Un año y diez meses, explica, está en la mitad superior de esa horquilla. Su batalla posterior fue otra: que Cortés "no se fuera de rositas". Según el abogado, el condenado se había declarado en concurso de acreedores y decía no tener ingresos. La acusación recurrió para que la suspensión de la pena de prisión quedara condicionada al pago efectivo de la indemnización, y lo consiguió. El paralelismo con Huelva es evidente: allí, la abogada Patricia Catalina tuvo que revertir la donación de la casa del agresor a su hijo para que las niñas cobraran. El caso todavía no está cerrado. "Estamos en fase de ejecución de sentencia", precisa. Empieza ahora el periodo de libertad vigilada, durante el cual Cortés tampoco podrá acercarse al joven ni comunicarse con él. El abogado valora la actitud del Valencia. El tutor de la residencia acompañó al jugador "tanto antes como durante y después", y el club "facilitó en todo momento que el joven pudiera seguir desarrollando su carrera profesional". De la Federación Española, en cambio, dice que no le consta ninguna actuación cerca del entorno del jugador más allá de la dimisión de Cortés, de la que no sabe "si fue una dimisión forzada". Hoy el joven sigue jugando al fútbol profesional. Necesitó ayuda psicológica, pero su abogado destaca "una madurez impropia de su edad". De todo el proceso, dice, se queda con dos cosas: "Que la verdad se debe defender siempre y ante cualquiera, y que tiene el apoyo incondicional de su familia y sus amigos". Cuando conoció la sentencia se sintió "feliz y aliviado al mismo tiempo", porque era el reconocimiento "en papel, tangible" de que había dicho la verdad. El lema está por toda la Ciutat Esportiva: "Educamos personas, formamos futbolistas". Detrás hay un Programa de Protección a la Infancia que, según explica a MARCA Borja Eroles, la Academia aplica "desde hace más de cinco temporadas". La última revisión llegó en 2025, con una auditoría externa que repasó sus puntos y formó a los profesionales de la Academia. El documento lo elaboraron sobre todo el área de Psicología de la Academia y el departamento legal del club. Eroles insiste en que no es un texto cerrado: "Se ha ido actualizando cada temporada en función de las situaciones que se van dando y de las modificaciones que puedan surgir en el ámbito legal". La prevención y la formación funcionan de forma permanente. Cuando surge un caso concreto, la comunicación llega por un canal de denuncias seguro a un responsable máximo, que la traslada al Comité. Allí se analiza y se decide qué medidas tomar según la gravedad, porque el protocolo distingue entre casos leves, graves y muy graves. El Comité lo forman hoy seis personas: dos miembros de la Dirección de la Academia, dos del departamento legal, el responsable de la Residencia y el responsable del área de Psicología. El protocolo obliga a todos los empleados que tratan con menores, desde tutores de residencia y entrenadores hasta delegados y ojeadores. También a quienes trabajan en el área Internacional y en las Escoles VCF, con campus, torneos y entrenamientos. Como exige la ley, todos los empleados que se relacionan con menores deben presentar el certificado negativo de delitos sexuales. El Valencia va un paso más allá con los proveedores habituales. Les pide que certifiquen, bajo su responsabilidad, que sus trabajadores tampoco tienen antecedentes de este tipo. Eroles pone ejemplos: chóferes de autobús, médicos o fisioterapeutas externos y vigilantes de seguridad. ¿Se puede mejorar? "Seguro", responde sin rodeos. El Comité, dice, está abierto a analizar lo que ocurre en su entorno y en otros clubes o sectores. La formación llega también de fuera, a través de LaLiga y de entidades como Kunina Sports, y se distribuye entre todos los profesionales de la Academia.
